cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width (manufacturer does not publish pixel pitch directly)
cameras.astro_notes: BSI Exmor R sensor, dual base ISO (base gain switch reported near ISO 500-640 by independent measurement, not manufacturer-stated). Max mechanical shutter 1/8000s; native Bulb mode plus in-camera Bulb Timer (set exposure length in menu, no external timer needed) on firmware from 2022 on. Built-in interval (time-lapse) shooting since launch. Long-exposure NR is a user-selectable menu toggle (dark-frame subtraction), commonly turned off for astro and replaced with manual darks. Star-eater raw spatial-filtering artifacts were substantially reduced from the a7 III generation onward per independent testing (Lonely Speck, Mark Shelley); the a7 IV was not flagged as a fresh regression in available 2023-2026 reporting, but no manufacturer statement confirms full elimination, so treat as improved-but-unverified. 5-axis IBIS rated 5.5 stops CIPA. No astro-modified (IR-removed) factory variant; third-party shops (Spencer's Camera, Kolari Vision) offer aftermarket IR/full-spectrum conversions for this body.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: Dual-gain BSI sensor; independent measurement (photonstophotos.net-style read-noise curves) places the low->high conversion-gain switch around ISO 640. Max shutter 1/8000s; supports Bulb. Built-in interval-shooting firmware added via v3.0 update in 2019 (originally shipped without one). Long-exposure NR toggle present, doubles capture time when enabled. This body is the one most frequently cited in 'star eater fixed in Mark III' reporting (PetaPixel 2018, Lonely Speck) after Sony's raw-processing change; still shows some spatial-filter softening on faint stars at very long bulb exposures per Mark Shelley's testing, less severe than a7 II generation. 5-axis IBIS rated 5.0 stops CIPA. No factory astro-modified version; aftermarket IR conversion available.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width; large photosite is the headline astro/low-light feature of this body
cameras.astro_notes: 12.1MP BSI sensor with an unusually large ~8.4 µm pixel pitch, giving strong per-pixel light-gathering and clean high-ISO files, at the cost of resolution for large prints. Dual-gain switch documented by DPReview measurement at approx. ISO 2000 in standard picture profiles (S-Log profiles shift the switch point, e.g. ISO 640/12800 in S-Log2/3 dual-base video modes; still-photo dual-gain ISO is not separately published by Sony). Max shutter 1/8000s, Bulb supported with in-camera Bulb Timer. Built-in interval shooting present. Long-exposure NR toggle available. Considered largely clear of the classic 'star eater' spatial-filter artifacts reported on earlier a7S/a7S II bodies. 5-axis IBIS rated 5.5 stops CIPA. No factory IR-modified version; third-party astro conversion available.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 60.2MP BSI sensor; small 3.76 µm pixel pitch means the NPF-rule exposure ceiling before star trailing is noticeably shorter than on lower-resolution bodies at the same focal length. Max shutter 1/8000s mechanical, Bulb supported with a native Bulb Timer (2s-900s / 15 min, set in menu, no external remote required) and separate 'Interval Shoot Func.' for time-lapses/star trails. Long-exposure NR toggle present. Cloudy Nights and other astro-forum testing (2023-2024) reports Sony 'made huge changes to the raw-data-filtering' on this body, i.e. the classic star-eater spatial filter is effectively gone or much reduced versus a7R III/IV, though this is community measurement, not a manufacturer claim. 8-axis IBIS rated 8.0 stops CIPA, the best in Sony's astro-relevant full-frame lineup. No factory IR-modified version; aftermarket conversion available.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width; shares the 33MP sensor used in the a7 IV
cameras.astro_notes: Compact-body sibling of the a7 IV with the same 33MP BSI sensor and Bionz XR processor plus an added AI processing unit for subject recognition (not astro-relevant). Native ISO 100-51,200 (extended 50-204,800). Max shutter 1/8000s with Bulb support. Built-in interval-shoot function present (introduced fleet-wide by this generation). Compact grip and smaller battery are the main practical trade-offs for long dark-sky sessions versus the standard a7 IV body, not a sensor difference. IBIS present; exact CIPA rating not confirmed from primary sources checked. No factory IR-modified version.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 50.1MP stacked-sensor flagship; astro-usable but not purpose-optimized for it (speed/AF flagship, not a low-light specialist like the a7S line). Max shutter 1/32000s electronic, 1/8000s mechanical, Bulb supported. Built-in interval shooting present. IBIS rated 8.5 stops CIPA, the highest in this survey. Cited by Capture the Atlas as an 'unbeatable all-rounder' for astro but flagged as more camera (and price) than most astro-only shooters need. No public reporting of star-eater regression found for this body as of the 2026 sources checked. No factory IR-modified version.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 24.5MP partially-stacked sensor (extra readout circuitry top/bottom, distinct from the fully stacked Z8/Z9 chip). Adds 'Starlight View' live-view boost and autofocus rated to -10 EV, both genuinely useful for framing/focusing under dark skies. Independent measurement (nikonrumors.com review analysis, 2024) finds base-ISO dynamic range about 0.82 EV lower than the Z6 II (10.44 EV vs 11.26 EV), a real trade-off for shadow-heavy blended nightscapes though the gap closes by roughly ISO 800. Nikon's older 'star eater' raw noise-reduction filtering is reported eliminated on this generation per Skies & Scopes. Max shutter 1/16,000s electronic / 1/8000s mechanical, Bulb supported. Built-in interval-timer shooting present. IBIS rated 8.0 stops CIPA. No factory IR-modified version; third-party conversion available.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 24.3MP conventional (non-stacked) BSI sensor, widely cited by astro reviewers (Skies & Scopes, PetaPixel) as the pick of the Z6 line for dark-sky work: higher base dynamic range than the Z6 III and no reported star-eater or sensor-banding issues. Max shutter 1/8000s, Bulb supported (fixes the original Z6's 30-second-only limitation cited in some early reviews). Built-in interval-timer shooting present. Long-exposure NR is a standard menu toggle. IBIS rated 5 stops CIPA. No factory IR-modified version; small flange distance makes it a popular third-party astro-conversion donor body.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 45.7MP fully stacked sensor shared with the Z9 flagship, brought into a smaller/lighter body. Fast readout essentially eliminates rolling-shutter concerns; not a primary astro selling point but relevant for star-trail time-lapse stacks. Max shutter 1/32000s electronic. Built-in intervalometer confirmed and usable together with extended (long) shutter speeds per DPReview forum documentation. Nikon's extended-ISO ceiling is not published for this body in the sources checked (recorded as null; do not guess). IBIS rated 6.0 stops CIPA. No factory IR-modified version; third-party conversion available at a premium given the body's cost.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width; shares the Z6 III-generation 24.5MP sensor in a retro-styled body
cameras.astro_notes: Retro-bodied 24.5MP full-frame camera with the same sensor generation as the Z6 III. Max shutter 1/8000s, Bulb supported. Built-in interval-timer shooting present (standard on this Z-series generation). Physical dials can be an ergonomic advantage for manual exposure work in the dark by feel, though this is a handling note rather than a sourced technical claim. IBIS rated 8 stops CIPA. No factory IR-modified version.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 24MP full-frame entry-level body, cited by Capture the Atlas as 'best budget full-frame' for Milky Way work, with the Starlight View low-light live-view assist inherited from the Z6 III/Z f generation. Max shutter 1/8000s mechanical / 1/2000s electronic (rolling-shutter-limited electronic ceiling, mechanical shutter is what matters for long exposures). Built-in interval-timer shooting present. IBIS rated 7.5 stops CIPA, unusually high for this price tier. No factory IR-modified version.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 45.7MP DSLR sensor still widely used and recommended secondhand for landscape astro/nightscapes; optical viewfinder has no live-view star-eater raw-filtering exposure since this predates Nikon's in-body raw processing changes seen on some Z bodies, though DSLR sensor-noise behavior is a separate topic from the mirrorless star-eater issue. Max shutter 1/8000s. Has a built-in intervalometer (interval timer shooting) in the DSLR menu system. Long-exposure NR toggle present, standard dark-frame-subtraction behavior, doubles capture time when enabled. No IBIS (optical SLR body, in-lens VR only). No factory IR-modified version from Nikon; a very common third-party astro-conversion donor body given its used-market price and pixel count.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 24.3MP DSLR, extremely popular secondhand nightscape body praised for near-ISO-invariant behavior (per multiple ISO-invariance write-ups, e.g. isoinvariance.com/DIYPhotography): astrophotographers commonly shoot at low ISO (e.g. ISO 200) to protect highlights and push exposure in post rather than raising in-camera ISO, with little quality penalty. Max shutter 1/4000s (notably slower top speed than the D850, irrelevant for long-exposure astro). Built-in intervalometer present in DSLR menu. No IBIS. No factory IR-modified version; common third-party astro-conversion donor body due to low used price.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 24.2MP sensor, large 6.0 µm pixel pitch favorable for the NPF rule and per-pixel noise. Max shutter 1/8000s standard, 1/16,000s electronic, Bulb supported. Canon's built-in interval timer shooting is limited to normal (max 30s) shutter speeds and cannot be combined with Bulb mode for multi-shot long exposures per Canon community documentation; a separate built-in Bulb Timer allows a single long exposure of arbitrary length but not a repeating sequence, so star-trail/time-lapse sequences beyond 30s per frame still need an external or app-based intervalometer. Long-exposure NR is a standard in-camera toggle. IBIS rated 8 stops CIPA. No factory IR-modified version; the discontinued EOS Ra (below) was Canon's dedicated astro body, built on the original EOS R, not this sensor generation.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: New 32.5MP sensor (a 25% linear-resolution jump over the R6 II's 24.2MP), announced 2025-11-05, so real-world astro track record is thin as of this 2026-09-27 check. Native ISO ceiling of 64,000 is lower than the R6 II's 102,400 native ceiling per manufacturer materials, a deliberate trade for the resolution increase; extended ISO figures vary slightly between outlets (50-102,800 per one spec sheet reviewed) and should be confirmed against Canon's own published spec page before shipping to users. 5-axis IBIS present; exact CIPA stop rating not confirmed from the sources checked (recorded as an open item, not guessed). Included here because it is the direct, current-model successor most 2025-2026 buying guides will point astro shoppers toward, even though it is too new to have accumulated the same body of independent astro field-testing as the R6 II.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width; shares the R6 II generation sensor
cameras.astro_notes: 24.2MP sensor shared with the R6 II generation, in Canon's lightest/cheapest full-frame mirrorless body, frequently cited (Capture the Atlas, PetaPixel) as the budget full-frame astro pick. No IBIS, a real trade-off for handheld work but irrelevant for tripod-mounted long exposures. Max shutter 1/4000s mechanical, 1/16,000s electronic; the slower mechanical top speed than the R6 II does not affect long-exposure astro use. Bulb mode supported. Long-exposure NR toggle present. No factory IR-modified version; single card slot and smaller battery are the other commonly cited trade-offs for extended night sessions.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 45MP stacked sensor, high-resolution flagship cited by Capture the Atlas among premium astro/general-purpose choices. Max shutter 1/8000s mechanical, 1/32000s electronic. Bulb Timer present for single long exposures; as with other Canon RF bodies, the built-in interval timer alone is capped at normal (sub-30s) shutter speeds for repeated frames. Long-exposure NR toggle present. IBIS rated 8.5 stops CIPA. No factory IR-modified version.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 30.3MP sensor, Canon's first full-frame mirrorless body and the donor platform for the astro-modified EOS Ra (see separate entry). No IBIS. Max shutter 1/8000s, Bulb supported. Long-exposure NR toggle present. Included here as the base/unmodified counterpart to the Ra so the two can be compared directly; general astro popularity of the plain EOS R specifically (vs. the R6/R8 successors) is modest in current 2025-2026 buying guides, included primarily for completeness against the Ra.

cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width; identical sensor size/resolution to the standard EOS R
cameras.astro_notes: DISCONTINUED, flagged per task instructions. Canon's dedicated astrophotography full-frame mirrorless body, announced Nov 2019 and discontinued by Canon in Sept 2021 (PetaPixel). Built on the standard EOS R body/sensor (30.3MP, same as above) but with a modified IR-cut filter passing roughly 4x more 656nm (hydrogen-alpha) transmission than the standard EOS R, aimed at emission-nebula reds; plus a live-view/EVF magnification of up to 30x for precise manual star focus. Otherwise shares the base EOS R's shutter, ISO, and lack-of-IBIS characteristics. No successor has been announced by Canon as of this 2026-09-27 check; Canon's current guidance points astro shooters toward standard R-series bodies plus third-party modification instead.

cameras.model: Lumix S5 II (and S5 IIX, stills-identical variant)
cameras.value_basis: derived from sensor width / resolution width
cameras.astro_notes: 24.2MP BSI sensor with Panasonic-documented Dual Native ISO (two hardware gain stages, not just a software switch), a feature Panasonic states explicitly in marketing/spec materials rather than one inferred only from third-party noise curves. On-sensor phase-detect AF (779 points) is a departure from Panasonic's older contrast-only AF and helps focus assistance in the dark. L-Mount is shared across Panasonic/Leica/Sigma. The S5 IIX is stills-identical to the S5 II (same sensor, ISO range, AF, burst rate); its differences are video-workflow features (ProRes/All-I recording, SSD output, streaming) that do not change astro stills capability, so it is not listed as a separate entry. IBIS rated 5 stops CIPA for the body alone (up to 6.5 stops with Dual IS using a stabilized lens), confirmed via Panasonic-sourced review coverage. Exact bulb/intervalometer menu behavior was not independently confirmed from a primary Panasonic spec page in this pass; treat as needing a follow-up check before publishing without further verification. No factory IR-modified version.
